case_studies.title: FedSkillGit: Federated Skill Evolution via Version Control
case_studies.abstract: Large language model agents can improve their capabilities by evolving reusable natural-language skills from execution experience. In real-world deployments, this experience is distributed across data owners who cannot pool their raw data, which motivates federated skill evolution. The natural first design lets each client evolve the whole skill document and upload the result for server-side aggregation. That design is poorly matched to skill evolution for three reasons. An evolved document can still carry client-specific content distilled from private traces, repeated transmission of a nearly
case_studies.summary: FedSkillGit tackles how to update shared LLM skills when data is split across organisations, building a version‑controlled framework that lets each client evolve parts of a skill and merge them without sharing raw data. The result is a privacy‑preserving, collaborative way to improve AI behaviour without centralising sensitive logs. This is not directly relevant to routine cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a federated approach to evolve language‑model skills using version control, which is novel for practitioners working with distributed LLM deployments. It has clear implications for MLOps and federated learning in SaaS contexts, offering potential for secure skill sharing across organisations. The methodology could be prototyped within 90 days by an IT team with existing version‑control and federated‑learning infrastructure, thus scoring above 30 on VALUE_90_DAYS. Overall scores: NOVELTY 25, IT_RELEVANCE 15, VALUE_90_DAYS 30, totaling 70. The paper is of interest to engineers but not immediately critical.}

case_studies.title: FDE-Gym: The Last Mile of AI Delivery
case_studies.abstract: Existing agent benchmarks typically evaluate agents on well-specified tasks defined by issue reports, specifications, or task tickets. Real-world customer delivery is different: forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) must clarify ambiguous requirements, work in live systems, and uncover unstated constraints. We introduce FDE-Gym, a benchmark of 95 end-to-end delivery tasks from 20 customer scenarios across 18 sectors, each adapted by industry experts from real-world delivery projects. case_studies.summary: FDE-Gym provides a realistic benchmark of 95 delivery tasks drawn from real customer projects, designed to test how well agents handle ambiguous requirements, live systems, and hidden constraints. It solves the problem of agents being evaluated only on tidy, pre‑defined tasks, by offering a more authentic testbed. The result is a set of 20 customer scenarios across 18 sectors that can be used to assess agent readiness in production environments.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: FDE-Gym offers a novel benchmark focused on realistic delivery tasks that could interest IT engineers looking to evaluate or build agentic systems for deployment, but it is still a research artifact with limited immediate applicability. Its relevance to infrastructure work is moderate, and it offers only marginal actionable guidance for a 90‑day build or risk flagging.

case_studies.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are expanding from assisting scientific research and engineering to autonomously developing and improving AI systems, advancing AI for AI (AI4AI) as a pathway toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). case_studies.title: Learning to Steer LLM Agents and Multi-Agent Systems
case_studies.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents and multi-agent systems increasingly tackle complex tasks through long-horizon tool use and inter-agent collaboration. However, these systems are prone to deviating from the overall goal as execution unfolds, which wastes execution resources and leads to undesired outcomes, a failure termed goal drift. In this work, we propose a steering agent that supervises execution on the fly and steers the system back on track when drift occurs. The steering agent observes the execution context, deciding when to intervene with a low-cost fast path and how to interve
case_studies.summary: Goal drift in large‑language‑model agents means they can stray from their overall objective during long‑run tasks, wasting resources and producing wrong outputs. The authors built a lightweight steering agent that watches an agent’s actions in real time, deciding when to step in with a quick corrective move to bring it back on track. The result is fewer missed goals and more efficient use of computation in multi‑agent setups.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM‑powered services, implement a monitoring layer that tracks agent decisions; when the context shows a deviation, trigger a low‑cost corrective routine, and log the intervention for future training. Check that your orchestration platform can inject such a steering agent without breaking existing pipelines.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a novel steering agent concept that addresses goal drift in LLM-based multi‑agent systems, which is a relevant issue for IT engineers deploying enterprise‑grade AI services. The idea is directly applicable to the design of agentic systems, LLM APIs, and DevOps pipelines that involve long‑horizon tool use, thereby scoring high on IT relevance. However, the practical deployment details are abstract, offering limited actionable guidance for immediate 90‑day implementation, resulting in a modest value score. The overall score exceeds 40, so "low_signal" is set to false.
